chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text:
A CELL is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms. It is the
smallest unit of life capable of performing all basic life functions independently.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Robert Hooke first observed cells in 1665 using a self-designed microscope while
examining a thin slice of cork.
Hooke called the box-like compartments "cells" (from the Latin word for "a little room").
Leeuwenhoek (1674) discovered free-living cells in pond water using an improved
microscope.
Robert Brown (1831) discovered the nucleus in cells.
Purkinje (1839) coined the term "protoplasm" for the fluid substance of the cell.
The CELL THEORY was presented by Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839): all plants
and animals are composed of cells and the cell is the basic unit of life.
Virchow (1855) expanded cell theory by stating that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Organisms made of a single cell are called UNICELLULAR (e.g., Amoeba, Chlamydomonas,
Paramecium, bacteria).
Organisms made of many cells are called MULTICELLULAR (e.g., fungi, plants, animals).

topics.topic_name: WHAT ARE LIVING ORGANISMS MADE UP OF?

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: (No further sub-topics; this is a single introductory topic)

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
All living organisms are made up of CELLS. A cell is the structural and functional
unit of life. Every cell arises from a pre-existing cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A cell is the smallest unit that can live on its own and carry out all basic functions
of life.
The shape and size of cells are related to their specific functions.
Some cells like Amoeba have changing shapes; nerve cells have a fixed, typical shape.
Every multicellular organism has come from a single cell. Cells divide to produce
cells of their own kind.
All cells come from pre-existing cells.
Cells of organisms show variety in shape and size but share common features:
plasma membrane, nucleus, and cytoplasm are found in almost every cell.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.1:
sections.aim: To prepare a temporary mount of onion peel and observe cells under microscope.
sections.materials:
Onion bulb, forceps, glass slide, water, safranin solution, cover slip,
compound microscope, mounting needle.
procedure: 1. Peel the skin (epidermis) from the concave side of an onion bulb using forceps.
2. Place the peel immediately in a watch glass containing water.
3. Put a drop of water on a glass slide and transfer a small flat piece of the peel.
4. Add a drop of safranin solution and cover with a cover slip (avoiding air bubbles).
5. Observe under low power and then high power of a compound microscope.
sections.observation:
Box-like cells with a prominent nucleus visible in each cell. All cells
look similar regardless of the size of onion they came from.
sections.conclusion:
Onion peel cells show a regular, brick-like pattern. The basic structure
of a cell is the same across different sizes of onions.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.2:
sections.aim: To prepare temporary mounts of different plant cells and compare their structure.
sections.materials:
Leaf peels, tip of roots, peels of onions of different sizes, glass slides,
safranin, microscope.
procedure: 1. Prepare temporary mounts of leaf peels, tip of roots, or peels of onions of
different sizes.
2. Observe and compare the cells.
sections.observation:
- Cells from different parts do not all look alike in terms of shape and size.
- But all cells look alike in basic structure (nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm).
sections.conclusion:
Cells from different parts of a plant body show differences in shape and
size but similarities in basic structure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Who discovered cells and how?
items.answer:
Robert Hooke discovered cells in 1665. He observed a thin slice of cork under a
self-designed microscope and noticed it resembled a honeycomb of many little
compartments, which he called "cells."

items.question: What is a unicellular organism? Give two examples.
items.answer:
An organism whose entire body is made up of a single cell is called a UNICELLULAR
organism. Examples: Amoeba and Paramecium.

items.question: State the cell theory as given by Schleiden and Schwann.
items.answer:
The cell theory states:
(i) All plants and animals are composed of cells.
(ii) The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
Virchow later added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

items.question: Who discovered the nucleus and who coined the term protoplasm?
items.answer:
Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in 1831. Purkinje coined the term "protoplasm"
in 1839 for the fluid substance of the cell.

items.question: Why is the cell called the structural and functional unit of life?
items.answer:
The cell is called the structural unit because all living organisms are made of
cells (it is the basic building block). It is called the functional unit because
all life processes (nutrition, respiration, excretion, reproduction) are carried
out within the cell.

items.question: What are multicellular organisms? Give two examples.
items.answer:
Organisms made of many cells, each performing specific functions, are called
MULTICELLULAR organisms. Examples: humans (animals) and mango trees (plants).

items.question: How did the discovery of electron microscope help in
items.answer:
Before the electron microscope, only basic cell structures (nucleus, cell membrane)
could be seen with light microscopes. With the electron microscope (discovered in
1940), scientists could observe the complex internal structure of cells and their
various organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus,
and lysosomes in fine detail. This greatly expanded knowledge of cell biology.

items.question: Why do cells of the same organism differ in shape and size?
items.answer:
Cells differ in shape and size because different cells are specialised to perform
different functions. The shape and size are directly related to the specific
function a cell performs. For example:
- Nerve cells are long to carry impulses over distances.
- Red blood cells are disc-shaped to carry oxygen efficiently.
- Muscle cells are elongated to allow contraction and relaxation.

items.question: "All cells come from pre-existing cells." Who proposed this and
items.answer:
Virchow (1855) proposed that all cells arise from pre-existing cells. This
significance of this statement is:
- It explains how organisms grow (cell division).
- It explains how organisms repair damaged tissues.
- It explains reproduction - all new organisms arise from existing cells
(gametes) of parent organisms.

items.question: A student observes onion peel cells of small and large
items.answer:
No, the cells will not look different in basic structure. Whether the onion is
small or large, the cells of the peel will have the same basic structure:
- A box-like shape with cell wall.
- A prominent nucleus.
- Cytoplasm.
- Cell membrane inside the cell wall.
This shows that cell structure is determined by the type of organism and type of
tissue, not by the size of the organism. The activity with onion peel confirms
this: cells from onions of different sizes look similar under the microscope.

items.question: How would you prepare a temporary mount of onion peel
items.answer:
Procedure:
1. Peel the epidermis from the concave side of an onion bulb using forceps.
2. Place it in a watch glass with water immediately.
3. Transfer a small, flat piece onto a glass slide with a drop of water.
4. Add a drop of safranin solution and place a cover slip carefully.
5. Observe under low power, then high power of a compound microscope.
Observation: Box-like cells arranged in rows, each with a prominent nucleus
stained red by safranin, cell wall visible as boundary, cytoplasm inside.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Who first observed and named cells?
items.explanation: Robert Hooke first observed cells in 1665 in cork and named them "cells." Leeuwenhoek discovered free-living cells; Brown discovered the nucleus.

items.question: The term "protoplasm" was coined by:
items.explanation: Purkinje coined "protoplasm" in 1839 for the fluid substance of the cell. Virchow stated cells arise from pre-existing cells; Brown discovered the nucleus.

items.question: Which of the following is a unicellular organism?
items.explanation: Amoeba is unicellular - its entire body is a single cell. Mango, earthworm, and frog are all multicellular organisms.

items.question: Cell theory was proposed by:
items.explanation: Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839) proposed cell theory. Virchow later added that cells arise from pre-existing cells.

items.question: The statement "all cells arise from pre-existing cells" was given by:
items.explanation: Virchow (1855) expanded cell theory with this statement. Schleiden and Schwann gave the original cell theory about cells being the basic unit of life.

items.question: Leeuwenhoek's contribution to cell biology was:

options.C: Discovery of free-living cells in pond water

items.explanation: Leeuwenhoek (1674) discovered free-living cells in pond water using an improved microscope. Hooke named cells; Brown discovered the nucleus.

items.question: Viruses are not considered living outside a host cell because:

options.B: They lack any membranes and cannot show life characteristics independently

items.explanation: Viruses lack membranes entirely and do not show characteristics of life until they enter a living cell and use its machinery. Membranes are essential for life processes.

items.question: Which microscope made it possible to study organelles in detail?
items.explanation: The electron microscope (1940) allowed observation of complex cell organelles like mitochondria and ER in fine detail. Compound microscope can show nucleus and cell membrane but not fine organelle structure.

items.question: In the onion peel activity, safranin is used to:

options.C: Stain cells so structures become visible

items.explanation: Safranin is a stain that colours certain cell structures (like nucleus and cell wall) so they become visible under the microscope. It does not kill or preserve cells.

items.question: A student prepares mounts from onion peels of two different-sized onions. Which observation is correct?

options.B: Smaller onion has more cells per unit area
options.C: Both show cells of similar basic structure
options.D: The number of nuclei per cell differs

items.explanation: Cell structure is determined by the type of tissue, not the size of the organism. Both small and large onion peel cells look structurally similar under the microscope - same box-like shape, nucleus, cell wall.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of cell theory?

options.A: All living organisms are made of cells
options.B: Cell is the basic unit of life
options.C: New cells arise from non-living matter
options.D: All cells arise from pre-existing cells

items.explanation: The idea that cells arise from non-living matter (spontaneous generation) was disproved. Cell theory states cells arise from pre-existing cells (Virchow). Options A, B, D are all part of the complete cell theory.

items.question: The shape of a nerve cell is long and branched. This is because:

options.B: Shape is related to the specific function the cell performs

items.explanation: The shape and size of cells are directly related to their specific functions. Nerve cells are long to carry impulses over large distances in the body. This is a fundamental principle of cell biology.

topics.topic_name: WHAT IS A CELL MADE UP OF? STRUCTURAL ORGANISATION OF A CELL

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A cell is organised into three main features: PLASMA MEMBRANE, NUCLEUS, and
CYTOPLASM. All activities inside the cell and interactions with the environment
are possible due to these features. In eukaryotic cells, membrane-bound organelles
are present inside the cytoplasm to carry out specialised functions.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: PROKARYOTIC CELLS: lack a defined nuclear membrane; nuclear region is called
NUCLEOID; membrane-bound organelles absent; generally small (1-10 micrometres).
Examples: bacteria.
EUKARYOTIC CELLS: have a well-defined nucleus surrounded by nuclear membrane;
membrane-bound organelles present; generally large (5-100 micrometres).
Examples: plant cells, animal cells, fungi.
Difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells:
Prokaryotic Cell            | Eukaryotic Cell
Size: generally small       | Size: generally large (5-100 micrometres)
(1-10 micrometres)          |
Nuclear region: poorly      | Nuclear region: well defined, surrounded
defined, no nuclear         | by nuclear membrane
membrane; called nucleoid   |
Chromosome: single          | Chromosome: more than one
Membrane-bound organelles:  | Membrane-bound organelles: present
absent                      |
The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of living organisms.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The PLASMA MEMBRANE (also called CELL MEMBRANE) is the outermost covering of
animal cells (and innermost in plant cells, lying inside the cell wall) that
separates the contents of the cell from its external environment.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: It is a SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE MEMBRANE - it allows the entry and exit of some
materials but prevents the movement of other materials.
It is flexible and made up of organic molecules called LIPIDS and PROTEINS.
The structure of the plasma membrane can be observed only through an electron
microscope.
The flexibility of the cell membrane enables the cell to engulf food and other
material from its external environment - this process is called ENDOCYTOSIS.
Amoeba acquires food through endocytosis.
Movement of substances across the membrane occurs by:
(a) DIFFUSION: spontaneous movement of a substance from a region of high
concentration to a region of low concentration. Example: CO2 moves out
of the cell; O2 enters the cell by diffusion.
(b) OSMOSIS: the net diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane
toward a higher solute concentration.
OSMOSIS - KEY CONCEPTS:
HYPOTONIC SOLUTION: outside solution has higher water concentration than the cell.
Water enters the cell by osmosis; cell swells.
ISOTONIC SOLUTION: outside solution has the same water concentration as the cell.
No net movement of water; cell stays the same size.
HYPERTONIC SOLUTION: outside solution has lower water concentration (more
concentrated) than the cell. Water moves out of the cell; cell shrinks.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.3:
sections.aim: To demonstrate osmosis using an egg.
sections.materials: Egg, dilute hydrochloric acid, pure water, concentrated salt solution.
procedure: (a) Remove the shell of an egg by dissolving in dilute hydrochloric acid. Place the
de-shelled egg in pure water and observe after 5 minutes.
(b) Place a similar de-shelled egg in concentrated salt solution and observe for
5 minutes.
sections.observation:
(a) The egg swells because water passes into it by osmosis (hypotonic solution
outside).
(b) The egg shrinks because water passes out of the egg into the salt solution
(hypertonic solution outside).
sections.conclusion:
Osmosis demonstrates the selectively permeable nature of the cell membrane.
Water moves from a region of higher water concentration to lower.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.4:
sections.aim: To observe osmosis in dried raisins or apricots.
sections.materials: Dried raisins or apricots, plain water, concentrated solution of sugar or salt.
procedure: 1. Put dried raisins or apricots in plain water and leave for some time.
2. Then place them in a concentrated solution of sugar or salt.
sections.observation:
(a) Each gains water and swells when placed in plain water (water enters by osmosis).
(b) When placed in concentrated solution, they lose water and shrink.
sections.conclusion:
Plant cells also absorb or lose water by osmosis depending on the
concentration of the surrounding solution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is a selectively permeable membrane?
items.answer:
A SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE MEMBRANE is one that allows the entry and exit of only
some materials while preventing the movement of others. The plasma membrane is
selectively permeable - it allows materials like O2, CO2 and water to pass
through but restricts other substances.

items.question: Define osmosis.
items.answer:
OSMOSIS is the net diffusion of water molecules across a selectively permeable
membrane from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a
region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution).

items.question: What are hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions? Give one
items.answer:
- HYPOTONIC SOLUTION: has higher water concentration than the cell. Effect:
water enters the cell by osmosis; cell swells (may burst in animal cells).
- ISOTONIC SOLUTION: has the same water concentration as the cell. Effect:
no net movement of water; cell maintains its size.
- HYPERTONIC SOLUTION: has lower water concentration (more concentrated) than
the cell. Effect: water moves out of cell; cell shrinks.

items.question: How does CO2 move in and out of the cell? Explain the process.
items.answer:
CO2 moves in and out of cells by the process of DIFFUSION.
- CO2 is a cellular waste product. It accumulates in high concentration inside
the cell during cellular respiration.
- The concentration of CO2 outside the cell (in blood/external environment) is
low compared to inside the cell.
- Due to this concentration difference, CO2 spontaneously moves from inside
the cell (high concentration) to outside (low concentration) through the
plasma membrane.
- Similarly, O2 enters the cell by diffusion when its concentration decreases
inside the cell (used in respiration), since O2 concentration outside is higher.
- Thus diffusion plays an important role in gaseous exchange.

items.question: Describe the structure and composition of the plasma membrane.
items.answer:
Structure and composition of the plasma membrane:
- It is the outermost covering of animal cells; in plant cells it lies inside
the cell wall.
- It is a SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE membrane.
- It is FLEXIBLE - this allows it to change shape.
- Composition: made of organic molecules called LIPIDS and PROTEINS.
- Its structure can only be observed through an electron microscope.
- Functions:
(i) Separates cell contents from external environment.
(ii) Regulates entry and exit of materials.
(iii) Its flexibility allows ENDOCYTOSIS (engulfing food - as in Amoeba).

items.question: With the help of the egg activity (Activity 5.3), explain osmosis and
items.answer:
The Egg Activity demonstrates osmosis:
Setup: The shell of an egg is dissolved in dilute hydrochloric acid, leaving
the thin outer membrane (selectively permeable) enclosing the egg.

Observation 1 - Egg in Pure Water:
- The egg swells because water concentration outside (pure water) is higher
than inside the egg.
- Water molecules move from outside (high concentration) to inside (low
concentration) through the membrane by osmosis.
- This is a HYPOTONIC solution condition.

Observation 2 - Egg in Concentrated Salt Solution:
- The egg shrinks because water concentration inside is higher than in the
concentrated salt solution.
- Water moves from inside the egg (high water concentration) to outside
(low water concentration).
- This is a HYPERTONIC solution condition.

Significance in Living Cells:
- Unicellular freshwater organisms and most plant cells gain water by osmosis.
- Water absorption by plant roots is an example of osmosis.
- If animal cells are placed in hypotonic solution, they swell and may burst.
- If plant cells are in hypertonic solution, water leaves and the cell shrinks
(plasmolysis occurs - cell contents contract away from cell wall).
- Osmosis maintains the water balance and turgidity of cells.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The plasma membrane is called selectively permeable because:

options.A: It allows all substances to pass
options.C: It allows entry and exit of only some materials
options.D: It only allows water to pass

items.explanation: The plasma membrane allows only certain materials to move in and out while blocking others, hence it is selectively permeable, not fully permeable or impermeable.

items.question: The movement of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a selectively permeable membrane is called:
items.explanation: Osmosis is the net diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane toward higher solute concentration. Diffusion is movement of any substance from high to low concentration.

items.question: The plasma membrane is made up of:
items.explanation: The plasma membrane is composed of organic molecules called lipids and proteins. Cellulose makes the cell wall in plants, not the plasma membrane.

items.question: A cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. What will happen?
items.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, the solute concentration outside is higher than inside the cell. Water moves out of the cell by osmosis, causing the cell to shrink. In a hypotonic solution, the cell would swell.

items.question: Amoeba obtains food by the process of:
items.explanation: Endocytosis is the process by which the flexible plasma membrane engulfs food particles. Amoeba uses this process. Osmosis and diffusion involve movement of molecules, not engulfing of food.

items.question: Dried raisins placed in plain water will:

options.A: Shrink due to loss of water
options.B: Swell due to entry of water by osmosis

items.explanation: Plain water is a hypotonic solution relative to raisins. Water enters the raisins by osmosis from high water concentration (plain water) to low water concentration (inside raisin), causing them to swell.

items.question: CO2 moves out of the cell and O2 moves into the cell by:
items.explanation: Both CO2 and O2 move by diffusion - from regions of higher concentration to lower concentration across the plasma membrane. CO2 (high inside, low outside) moves out; O2 (high outside, low inside) moves in. No energy is required.

items.question: The structure of the plasma membrane can be observed only through:
items.explanation: The plasma membrane is extremely thin and its detailed structure (lipid bilayer with proteins) can only be observed through an electron microscope. A compound microscope can show the cell outline but not the membrane structure.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The CELL WALL is a rigid outer covering found in plant cells, fungi, and bacteria,
lying outside the plasma membrane. It provides structural support and protection
to the cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Present in: plant cells, fungi, and bacteria. ABSENT in animal cells.
The plant cell wall is mainly composed of CELLULOSE - a complex substance that
provides structural strength to plants.
FUNCTIONS of cell wall:
(i) Provides shape and rigidity to plant cells.
(ii) Protects the cell from mechanical injury.
(iii) Allows plant cells to withstand hypotonic (very dilute) external media
without bursting - because when the cell swells, the cell wall exerts
an equal and opposite pressure (wall pressure) on the swollen cell.
(iv) Prevents invasion by parasitic fungi.
PLASMOLYSIS: When a plant cell loses water through osmosis (in hypertonic
solution), the cell contents (cytoplasm) shrink and move away from the cell wall.
This phenomenon is called PLASMOLYSIS.
In some plants like desert plants, the epidermis has a thick waxy coating of
CUTIN on its outer surface (waterproofing quality).
As plants grow older, secondary meristem (outer layer of cortex) forms layers
of cells which constitute the CORK. Cork cells are dead, compactly arranged
without intercellular spaces, and have a substance called SUBERIN in their
walls making them impervious to gases and water.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.5:
sections.aim: To observe plasmolysis in Rhoeo leaf cells.
sections.materials:
Rhoeo leaf, glass slide, cover slip, concentrated sugar/salt solution,
microscope.
procedure: 1. Mount the peel of a Rhoeo leaf in water on a slide.
2. Examine under high power of a microscope. Note the small green granules
(chloroplasts) and the coloured cell sap in vacuoles.
3. Put a strong solution of sugar or salt on the mounted leaf on the slide.
Wait a minute and observe.
4. Now place some Rhoeo leaves in boiling water for a few minutes (kills cells).
Then mount and add strong sugar/salt solution, observe.
sections.observation:
- In step 3, the chloroplasts and cell contents move away from the cell wall
(plasmolysis occurs) in living cells.
- In step 4, no plasmolysis occurs in boiled (dead) cells.
sections.conclusion:
Only living cells can absorb water by osmosis. Dead cells cannot show
plasmolysis, confirming plasmolysis is a life process requiring
a functioning selectively permeable membrane.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is plasmolysis?
items.answer:
PLASMOLYSIS is the phenomenon in which a living plant cell loses water through
osmosis when placed in a hypertonic (concentrated) solution. As water moves out,
the cell contents (cytoplasm and vacuole) shrink and the plasma membrane
contracts away from the cell wall.

items.question: Why can plant cells withstand hypotonic solutions without bursting,
items.answer:
Plant cells have a rigid CELL WALL made of cellulose outside the plasma membrane.
When a plant cell is placed in a hypotonic solution, water enters by osmosis and
the cell swells. However:
- The cell wall builds up a wall pressure (turgor pressure) equal and opposite to
the osmotic pressure.
- This prevents the cell from bursting.
- Animal cells lack a cell wall, so when water enters by osmosis in a hypotonic
solution, there is nothing to resist the swelling and the animal cell bursts.

items.question: Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall in plant cells.
items.answer:
Structure:
- The cell wall is a rigid, outer covering lying outside the plasma membrane.
- It is mainly composed of CELLULOSE, a complex carbohydrate that provides
structural strength.
- The plant cell wall is non-living.
Functions:
(i) Gives definite shape and mechanical support to plant cells.
(ii) Protects cells from mechanical injury and infection by parasitic fungi.
(iii) Allows plant cells to withstand hypotonic media without bursting by
developing wall pressure (turgor pressure).
(iv) Cork cells (secondary cell wall with suberin) protect against gas and
water loss in older plant parts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The cell wall of plant cells is mainly composed of:
items.explanation: Plant cell walls are mainly composed of cellulose, which provides structural strength. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls; suberin is found in cork cells; lignin in woody plants.

items.question: Which of the following does NOT have a cell wall?
items.explanation: Animal cells lack a cell wall entirely - they have only a plasma membrane as the outer covering. Plant cells, bacteria, and fungi all have cell walls (though of different composition).

items.question: When a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution, it:
items.explanation: In a concentrated (hypertonic) salt solution, water moves out of the plant cell by osmosis. The cell contents shrink away from the cell wall - this is called plasmolysis. The cell does not burst because the cell wall is rigid.

items.question: Cork cells are impervious to gases and water because their walls contain:
items.explanation: Cork cells have a substance called suberin in their walls that makes them impervious to gases and water. Cork cells are dead and compactly arranged without intercellular spaces, making them excellent protective tissue.

items.question: In the Rhoeo leaf activity, boiled cells did not show plasmolysis when placed in concentrated solution because:

options.B: Boiling increases the solute concentration inside cells
options.C: Boiling kills cells, destroying the selective permeability of the membrane

items.explanation: Plasmolysis requires a living, selectively permeable plasma membrane. Boiling kills cells and destroys the selective permeability of the membrane, so water can freely move in and out without the controlled osmosis that causes plasmolysis. This confirms plasmolysis is a life process.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The NUCLEUS is a large, spherical or oval organelle surrounded by a double-layered
nuclear membrane, found in eukaryotic cells. It is the control centre of the cell
that directs all cellular activities and contains the genetic material (DNA).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The nucleus has a double-layered covering called the NUCLEAR MEMBRANE.
The nuclear membrane has PORES (nuclear pores) which allow transfer of material
between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
The nucleus contains CHROMOSOMES - rod-shaped structures visible only when the
cell is about to divide.
CHROMOSOMES contain information for inheritance of characters from parents to
next generation in the form of DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid) molecules.
Chromosomes are composed of DNA and PROTEIN.
DNA molecules contain the information necessary for constructing and organising
cells. Functional segments of DNA are called GENES.
In a non-dividing cell, DNA is present as part of CHROMATIN material - visible
as entangled mass of thread-like structures.
The nucleus plays a central role in CELLULAR REPRODUCTION (cell division).
The nucleus determines how the cell will develop and what form it will exhibit at
maturity by directing the chemical activities of the cell.
In PROKARYOTES (bacteria), the nuclear region is poorly defined - lacks a nuclear
membrane. This undefined nuclear region containing only nucleic acids is called
the NUCLEOID. Such organisms are called PROKARYOTES.
Organisms with cells having a nuclear membrane are called EUKARYOTES.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.6 (NUCLEUS OBSERVATION):
sections.aim: To observe nucleus in cheek cells.
sections.materials:
Glass slide, ice-cream spoon, methylene blue solution, cover slip,
microscope.
procedure: 1. Take a glass slide with a drop of water. Use an ice-cream spoon to gently scrape
the inside of the cheek.
2. Transfer the material (cheek cells) to the slide and spread evenly.
3. Add a drop of methylene blue solution, place cover slip.
4. Observe under microscope.
sections.observation:
Irregular-shaped cells with a nucleus visible in the centre of each cell.
Different shape from onion peel cells (onion cells are box-like while
cheek cells are irregular).
sections.conclusion:
Human cheek cells (animal cells) have a clearly visible nucleus,
confirming the presence of nucleus in eukaryotic cells.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is the nucleoid?
items.answer:
NUCLEOID is the poorly defined nuclear region in prokaryotic cells (like bacteria)
that lacks a nuclear membrane. It contains only nucleic acids (DNA) without being
enclosed by a membrane. Organisms with nucleoid are called prokaryotes.

items.question: Describe the structure of the nucleus and state its functions.
items.answer:
Structure of nucleus:
- Large, spherical or oval organelle in the cytoplasm.
- Surrounded by a double-layered NUCLEAR MEMBRANE with nuclear pores.
- Contains CHROMOSOMES made of DNA and protein.
- In non-dividing cells, DNA is present as CHROMATIN material.
Functions:
(i) Controls all metabolic activities of the cell.
(ii) Contains genetic information (DNA/genes) for inheritance.
(iii) Plays central role in cell division (cellular reproduction).
(iv) Determines how a cell develops and what form it takes.

items.question: What are chromosomes? What is their significance?
items.answer:
CHROMOSOMES are rod-shaped structures visible in the nucleus when the cell is
about to divide. Their structure and significance:
- Made of DNA and protein molecules.
- DNA contains the information necessary for constructing and organising cells.
- Functional segments of DNA are called GENES.
- Chromosomes carry information for inheritance of characters from parents to
offspring.
- The number of chromosomes is fixed for each species (e.g., humans have 46
chromosomes = 23 pairs).
- In non-dividing cells, chromosomes exist as CHROMATIN material (entangled
thread-like structures) and become organised into distinct chromosomes only
during cell division.
- Significance: they are the physical carriers of hereditary information.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The nucleus is surrounded by a:
items.explanation: The nucleus is surrounded by a double-layered nuclear membrane with nuclear pores that allow material transfer between nucleus and cytoplasm. A single membrane is not accurate for the nucleus.

items.question: Functional segments of DNA are called:
items.explanation: Genes are the functional segments of DNA that carry information for specific characteristics. Chromosomes are made of DNA and protein; chromatin is the dispersed form of chromosomes; nucleoid is found in prokaryotes.

items.question: Which organelle contains two organelles that have their own DNA and ribosomes?
items.explanation: Mitochondria and plastids are unique in having their own DNA and ribosomes, making them capable of synthesising some of their own proteins. This is why they are called strange organelles.

items.question: Prokaryotes are different from eukaryotes in that:
items.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a defined nuclear membrane; their genetic material is in a region called nucleoid. Eukaryotes have a well-defined nucleus with nuclear membrane. Prokaryotes are generally smaller than eukaryotes.

items.question: Chromosomes are visible as rod-shaped structures:

options.B: Only in non-dividing cells as chromatin
options.C: Only when the cell is about to divide

items.explanation: In non-dividing cells, chromosomes exist as dispersed chromatin material (entangled threads). Chromosomes become organised into distinct, visible rod-shaped structures only when the cell is about to divide. Both animal and plant cells show this.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
CYTOPLASM is the fluid content inside the plasma membrane (and outside the nucleus).
It is the semi-fluid, jelly-like material that fills the cell and contains many
specialised cell organelles.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: When we observe temporary mounts of onion peel or human cheek cells, a large region
of each cell enclosed by the cell membrane is visible - this takes up very little
stain; it is called CYTOPLASM.
The cytoplasm is the fluid content inside the plasma membrane.
It contains many specialised cell ORGANELLES which each perform a specific function.
Cell organelles are enclosed by membranes (in eukaryotic cells).
In PROKARYOTES, beside the absence of a defined nuclear region:
membrane-bound organelles are also absent.
The chlorophyll in photosynthetic prokaryotic bacteria is associated with
membranous vesicles (bag-like structures) but NOT with plastids.
In EUKARYOTES, cells have nuclear membrane as well as membrane-enclosed organelles.
The significance of membranes: Viruses lack any membranes and hence do not show
characteristics of life until they enter a living body and use its cell machinery.

items.question: What is cytoplasm?
items.answer:
CYTOPLASM is the fluid content inside the plasma membrane and outside the nucleus.
It is a semi-fluid, jelly-like material that fills the cell and contains many
specialised membrane-bound organelles, each performing specific functions for
the cell.

items.question: What is the significance of membranes in cells? Why do viruses not
items.answer:
Significance of membranes:
- Membranes create separate compartments for different chemical reactions.
- They control movement of substances in and out of organelles and the cell.
- They allow specialised reactions to occur in specific locations (e.g., ATP
synthesis in mitochondria).
Viruses and membranes:
- Viruses completely lack any membranes.
- Without membranes, viruses cannot carry out any life processes independently
(no metabolism, no ATP production, no protein synthesis on their own).
- They only show characteristics of life when they enter a living cell and
use the cell's machinery to reproduce.
- This demonstrates that membranes are fundamental to life.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Cytoplasm is the fluid present:

options.B: Inside the plasma membrane and outside the nucleus

items.explanation: Cytoplasm is the fluid content inside the plasma membrane (outer boundary) and outside the nucleus. It is found in both plant and animal cells.

items.question: In prokaryotic cells, the chlorophyll for photosynthesis is associated with:
items.explanation: In photosynthetic prokaryotic bacteria, chlorophyll is associated with membranous vesicles (bag-like structures), NOT with plastids (chloroplasts), because prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles.

items.question: Which of the following is true about cell organelles in prokaryotes?

options.C: Nucleus is present but without membrane

items.explanation: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles. They also lack a defined nuclear membrane. Their nuclear region is called nucleoid and contains only nucleic acids without a surrounding membrane.

items.question: The cytoplasm takes up very little stain when cells are prepared for microscopy. This is because:

options.B: It is a fluid-like material without large organelles to stain

items.explanation: The cytoplasm is a semi-fluid, jelly-like material. It does not have large, stain-absorbing structures uniformly distributed throughout, so it appears lightly or unstained compared to the nucleus (which stains darkly with iodine or safranin due to dense chromatin/DNA).

items.question: Why do viruses not show characteristics of life outside a host cell?
items.explanation: Viruses lack any membranes entirely. Membranes are fundamental to all life processes - they create compartments for reactions, control substance movement, and enable energy production. Without membranes, viruses cannot perform any life processes and are essentially non-living outside a host cell.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
CELL ORGANELLES are small, specialised structures within the cytoplasm of eukaryotic
cells, each enclosed by a membrane and performing a specific function. They are the
"little organs" of the cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Each of the membrane-bound organelles performs a specific function.
Large and complex cells (multicellular organisms) need organelles to separate
different chemical activities.
Key organelles: endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes,
mitochondria, plastids, and vacuoles.
Only mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (ER) is a large network of membrane-bound tubes and
sheets present in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. It serves as a transport
system and manufacturing surface within the cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The ER membrane is similar in structure to the plasma membrane.
TWO TYPES of ER:
(a) ROUGH ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (RER): has ribosomes attached to its surface;
appears rough under electron microscope; involved in PROTEIN SYNTHESIS and
transport.
(b) SMOOTH ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (SER): lacks ribosomes; involved in manufacture
of FAT MOLECULES (lipids) important for cell function; in liver cells of
vertebrates, SER plays a crucial role in DETOXIFYING many poisons and drugs.
FUNCTIONS of ER:
(i) Serves as channels for transport of materials between various regions of
cytoplasm and between cytoplasm and nucleus.
(ii) Functions as a manufacturing surface (RER for proteins; SER for lipids).
(iii) Proteins and lipids help in building the cell membrane - process known as
MEMBRANE BIOGENESIS.
(iv) Some proteins and lipids produced by ER function as enzymes and hormones.
(v) Provides a cytoplasmic framework (structural support).
The ER always forms a network system in the cell.
Ribosomes (present on RER) are the sites of PROTEIN MANUFACTURE in all active cells.
SUB-TOPIC 5.2.5(i) Q&A
Q1 [2 Marks]: What is the difference between RER and SER?
A1: ROUGH ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (RER): has ribosomes attached to its surface; appears
rough; involved in protein synthesis and transport.
SMOOTH ENDOPLASMIC RETICULUM (SER): lacks ribosomes; involved in manufacture of
fat molecules (lipids); in liver cells it detoxifies poisons and drugs.
Q2 [3 Marks]: State the functions of the endoplasmic reticulum.
A2: Functions of endoplasmic reticulum:
(i) Transport channels: serve as channels for transport of materials between
cytoplasm regions and between cytoplasm and nucleus.
(ii) Manufacturing surface: RER manufactures proteins; SER manufactures lipids.
(iii) Membrane biogenesis: proteins and lipids produced help build the cell membrane.
(iv) Produce enzymes and hormones.
(v) SER detoxifies poisons and drugs in liver cells.
(vi) Provides structural framework (cytoplasmic skeleton) for the cell.
Q3 [4 Marks]: Explain how the endoplasmic reticulum helps in membrane biogenesis.
A3: Membrane biogenesis by endoplasmic reticulum:
The ER manufactures PROTEINS (by RER with ribosomes) and LIPIDS (by SER).
These manufactured proteins and lipids are the main components of ALL cellular
membranes, including the plasma membrane and the membranes of organelles.
The proteins and lipids produced by the ER are transported to their destinations
(including the cell membrane) via the ER transport channels and Golgi apparatus.
This process of building new membrane material is called MEMBRANE BIOGENESIS.
Thus, the ER acts as both a factory and a transport system for the raw
materials needed to construct and maintain all membranes in the cell.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The GOLGI APPARATUS (also called Golgi body or Golgi complex) is a system of
membrane-bound vesicles (flattened sacs called cisterns) arranged in stacks,
approximately parallel to each other.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: First described by CAMILLO GOLGI (born 1843 in Corteno near Brescia, Italy).
Golgi apparatus consists of a system of membrane-bound vesicles (FLATTENED SACS)
arranged in stacks called CISTERNS.
The membranes of Golgi apparatus often have connections with the membranes of ER
they constitute another portion of a complex cellular membrane system.
FUNCTIONS of Golgi apparatus:
(i) STORAGE: stores the material synthesised near the ER.
(ii) MODIFICATION: modifies materials received from ER.
(iii) PACKAGING: packages products in vesicles and dispatches them to various
targets inside and outside the cell.
(iv) In some cases, COMPLEX SUGARS may be made from simple sugars in the Golgi
apparatus.
(v) INVOLVED IN FORMATION OF LYSOSOMES.
Material synthesised near the ER is packaged and dispatched to various targets
inside and outside the cell through the Golgi apparatus.
DO YOU KNOW?
Camillo Golgi received the Nobel Prize in 1906 (shared with Santiago Ramón y Cajal)
for their work on the structure of the nervous system. Golgi developed a revolutionary
method of staining individual nerve and cell structures using a weak solution of
silver nitrate (called the "black reaction").
SUB-TOPIC 5.2.5(ii) Q&A
Q1 [2 Marks]: What are the functions of the Golgi apparatus?
A1: Functions of Golgi apparatus:
(i) Stores, modifies, and packages materials synthesised near the ER.
(ii) Dispatches packaged materials (in vesicles) to targets inside and outside
the cell.
(iii) Synthesis of complex sugars from simple sugars.
(iv) Involved in formation of lysosomes.
Q2 [3 Marks]: Describe the structure of the Golgi apparatus and explain why it is
considered part of the cellular membrane system.
A2: Structure of Golgi apparatus:
Consists of a system of membrane-bound vesicles (flattened sacs) called CISTERNS.
These cisterns are arranged approximately parallel to each other in stacks.
The membranes of the Golgi apparatus often have connections with the membranes
of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
Why it is part of the cellular membrane system:
The ER produces proteins and lipids, passes them to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, packages and dispatches them.
Since ER and Golgi membranes are connected and work together in a coordinated
transport system, they collectively constitute a complex cellular membrane system.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
LYSOSOMES are membrane-bound sacs filled with powerful digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes
capable of breaking down all organic material. They act as the waste disposal system
of the cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Lysosomes are a kind of WASTE DISPOSAL SYSTEM of the cell.
They contain powerful DIGESTIVE ENZYMES made by RER.
Functions:
(i) Keep the cell clean by DIGESTING any foreign material (bacteria, food) entering
the cell.
(ii) Digest WORN-OUT CELL ORGANELLES (cellular debris).
(iii) Break down COMPLEX SUBSTANCES into simpler ones.
SUICIDE BAGS: During disturbance in cellular metabolism (e.g., when the cell gets
damaged), lysosomes may BURST and the digestive enzymes are released. These
enzymes then digest their own cell - this is why lysosomes are called the
"SUICIDE BAGS" of the cell.
SUB-TOPIC 5.2.5(iii) Q&A
Q1 [2 Marks]: Why are lysosomes called "suicide bags"?
A1: Lysosomes are called SUICIDE BAGS because during disturbance in cellular
metabolism or when a cell is damaged, lysosomes may burst. The powerful digestive
enzymes released then digest the entire cell itself, causing cell death - hence
the term "suicide bags."
Q2 [3 Marks]: Describe the structure and functions of lysosomes.
A2: Structure: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs in the cytoplasm filled with powerful
hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes. The enzymes are made by RER.
Functions:
(i) Clean the cell by digesting foreign material (bacteria, food particles)
entering the cell.
(ii) Remove worn-out cell organelles and cellular debris by digesting them.
(iii) Break down complex substances into simpler ones.
(iv) In abnormal conditions, lysosomal enzymes are released into the cytoplasm
and digest the cell itself (suicide bags).

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
MITOCHONDRIA (singular: mitochondrion) are double membrane-bound organelles known
as the POWERHOUSES OF THE CELL because they produce ATP (Adenosine triphosphate),
the energy currency of the cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Known as the POWERHOUSES OF THE CELL.
Have TWO MEMBRANE COVERINGS:
OUTER MEMBRANE: porous (has pores).
INNER MEMBRANE: deeply folded; these folds are called CRISTAE and increase the
surface area for ATP-generating chemical reactions.
The energy required for various chemical activities needed for life is released
by mitochondria in the form of ATP molecules.
ATP is known as the ENERGY CURRENCY OF THE CELL.
The body uses energy stored in ATP for making new chemical compounds and for
mechanical work.
UNIQUE FEATURE: Mitochondria are STRANGE ORGANELLES - they have their own DNA
and RIBOSOMES. Therefore, mitochondria are able to MAKE SOME OF THEIR OWN
PROTEINS.
SUB-TOPIC 5.2.5(iv) Q&A
Q1 [2 Marks]: Why are mitochondria called the powerhouses of the cell?
A1: Mitochondria are called POWERHOUSES OF THE CELL because they produce ATP
(Adenosine triphosphate), which is the energy currency of the cell. The energy
required for all chemical activities and mechanical work in the cell is released
by mitochondria in the form of ATP.
Q2 [3 Marks]: Describe the structure of mitochondria. Why are they called "strange"
organelles?
A2: Structure of mitochondria:
Have two membrane coverings.
Outer membrane: porous.
Inner membrane: deeply folded into CRISTAE which increase surface area for
ATP-generating reactions.
Why they are called strange:
Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes.
Because of this, mitochondria are able to make some of their own proteins.
Having their own genetic material (DNA) and protein synthesis machinery
(ribosomes) inside an organelle is unusual and makes them "strange" compared
to most other organelles which depend entirely on the nucleus.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
PLASTIDS are large membrane-bound organelles found ONLY in PLANT CELLS. They are
of two main types: CHROMOPLASTS (coloured) and LEUCOPLASTS (white or colourless).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Present ONLY in PLANT CELLS; absent in animal cells.
TWO TYPES:
(a) CHROMOPLASTS: coloured plastids.
Those containing the green pigment CHLOROPHYLL are called CHLOROPLASTS.
Chloroplasts are important for PHOTOSYNTHESIS in plants.
Chloroplasts also contain various yellow or orange pigments in addition
to chlorophyll.
(b) LEUCOPLASTS: white or colourless plastids.
Primary function is STORAGE.
Materials such as starch, oils, and protein granules are stored in
leucoplasts.
INTERNAL ORGANISATION of Chloroplast:
Consists of numerous MEMBRANE LAYERS embedded in a material called STROMA.
Similar to mitochondria in external structure.
UNIQUE FEATURE: Like mitochondria, plastids also have their own DNA and ribosomes.
SUB-TOPIC 5.2.5(v) Q&A
Q1 [2 Marks]: What are chromoplasts and leucoplasts?
A1: CHROMOPLASTS are coloured plastids found in plant cells.
Those containing chlorophyll (green pigment) are called CHLOROPLASTS -
important for photosynthesis.
LEUCOPLASTS are white or colourless plastids found in plant cells.
Their primary function is STORAGE of starch, oils, and protein granules.
Q2 [3 Marks]: Compare mitochondria and plastids, highlighting their similarities.
A2: Similarities between mitochondria and plastids:
(i) Both are membrane-bound organelles (double membrane).
(ii) Both have their own DNA and ribosomes, allowing them to synthesise some
of their own proteins - making them "strange" organelles.
(iii) Internal organisation: both have numerous membrane layers embedded in a
matrix (stroma in chloroplast; matrix in mitochondria).
(iv) Both are important energy-related organelles - mitochondria for cellular
respiration (ATP production), chloroplasts for photosynthesis (light
energy capture).
Difference: Plastids are found ONLY in plant cells; mitochondria are found in
both plant and animal cells.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: VACUOLES are storage sacs for solid or liquid contents within the cell.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: ANIMAL CELLS: vacuoles are SMALL in size.
PLANT CELLS: vacuoles are VERY LARGE; the CENTRAL VACUOLE of some plant cells may
occupy 50-90% of the cell volume.
In plant cells, vacuoles are full of CELL SAP and provide TURGIDITY and RIGIDITY
to the cell.
Many substances of importance in the life of the plant cell are stored in
vacuoles, including: amino acids, sugars, various organic acids, and some proteins.
In SINGLE-CELLED ORGANISMS like Amoeba:
The food vacuole contains the food items that Amoeba has consumed.
Some unicellular organisms have specialised vacuoles that play important roles
in EXPELLING EXCESS WATER and some wastes from the cell.
SUB-TOPIC 5.2.5(vi) Q&A
Q1 [2 Marks]: How are vacuoles in plant cells different from those in animal cells?
A1: In ANIMAL CELLS, vacuoles are SMALL in size.
In PLANT CELLS, vacuoles are VERY LARGE; the central vacuole may occupy
50-90% of the cell volume. Plant cell vacuoles are filled with cell sap and
provide turgidity and rigidity to the cell, and store important substances
like amino acids and sugars.
Q2 [3 Marks]: What are the functions of vacuoles in plant cells and in unicellular
organisms?
A2: Functions of vacuoles:
In plant cells:
(i) Provide TURGIDITY and RIGIDITY to the cell (filled with cell sap).
(ii) STORAGE of important substances: amino acids, sugars, organic acids,
proteins.
(iii) Store waste products.
In unicellular organisms (like Amoeba):
(i) FOOD VACUOLE: stores food items that Amoeba has consumed.
(ii) CONTRACTILE VACUOLE: specialised vacuole that plays important role in
expelling excess water and waste products from the cell.

sections.label: TOPIC 5.2 Q&A (Overall - covering Cell Structure and Organelles)

items.question: Name the two types of endoplasmic reticulum and state one
Which organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell and why?
items.answer:
MITOCHONDRIA are called the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP
(Adenosine triphosphate) - the energy currency of the cell - through cellular
respiration. This ATP energy is used for all cellular activities and mechanical work.

items.question: Name two organelles that contain their own genetic material
items.answer:
MITOCHONDRIA and PLASTIDS (chloroplasts) are the two organelles that have their
own DNA and ribosomes, enabling them to synthesise some of their own proteins.

items.question: What is the primary function of leucoplasts?
items.answer:
The primary function of LEUCOPLASTS is STORAGE. They store materials such as
starch, oils, and protein granules. Leucoplasts are white or colourless plastids
found only in plant cells.

items.question: Why are lysosomes called the waste disposal system of the cell?
items.answer:
Lysosomes are called the waste disposal system because they contain powerful
digestive enzymes that break down and digest:
(i) Foreign materials (bacteria, food particles) entering the cell.
(ii) Worn-out organelles and cellular debris.
Thus they keep the cell clean by removing waste materials.

items.question: What is membrane biogenesis?
items.answer:
MEMBRANE BIOGENESIS is the process of building new cell membranes. The ER produces
proteins (by RER) and lipids (by SER). These proteins and lipids are the main
components of all cellular membranes. They are dispatched via Golgi apparatus to
build and maintain all membranes in the cell.

items.question: If the organisation of a cell is destroyed due to a physical
items.answer:
If cell organisation is destroyed:
- The plasma membrane will lose its selective permeability - uncontrolled
movement of substances will occur.
- Lysosomes may burst (since their membrane is damaged), releasing digestive
enzymes into the cytoplasm, which will digest cell components - causing
cell death.
- Mitochondria will be destroyed, stopping ATP production - all energy-requiring
processes (active transport, movement, synthesis) will stop.
- The nucleus will lose control over cell activities - protein synthesis stops.
- Overall result: the cell will die as it can no longer maintain homeostasis
or carry out life functions.

items.question: What would happen to the life of a cell if there was no
items.answer:
Without Golgi apparatus:
- Proteins synthesised by RER and lipids by SER cannot be stored, modified
or packaged for dispatch.
- Secretion of materials outside the cell will stop completely.
- Lysosomes cannot form (Golgi is involved in lysosome formation), so waste
disposal in the cell will fail.
- Complex sugars cannot be formed from simple sugars.
- Membrane biogenesis will be severely affected since processed membrane
materials cannot be dispatched.
- Overall: cellular communication, secretion, and waste management will fail.

items.question: Why are plastids present only in plant cells? What advantage
items.answer:
Plastids are present only in plant cells because plants are autotrophs (can make
their own food) and need specialised organelles for:
- CHLOROPLASTS for photosynthesis (capturing light energy to make glucose).
- LEUCOPLASTS for storage of food materials (starch, oils, proteins).
Animal cells are heterotrophs (obtain food from outside) and do not need
organelles for food production or large food storage.
Advantage to plants:
- Chloroplasts allow plants to produce food using sunlight (photosynthesis).
- Leucoplasts store reserve food materials.
- Chromoplasts (other colours) attract insects for pollination.

items.question: Compare plant cell and animal cell based on their
items.answer:
Feature              | Plant Cell              | Animal Cell
---------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------
Cell wall            | Present (cellulose)     | Absent
Chloroplasts         | Present                 | Absent
Vacuoles             | Very large central      | Small and few
| vacuole (50-90% cell)   |
Plastids             | Present (chloroplasts,  | Absent
| leucoplasts)            |
Plasma membrane      | Present (inside wall)   | Present (outer boundary)
Nucleus              | Present (eukaryotic)    | Present (eukaryotic)
Mitochondria         | Present                 | Present
Golgi apparatus      | Present                 | Present
Lysosomes            | Rarely present          | Commonly present
Shape                | Generally fixed,        | Variable shape
| box-like                | (no rigid wall)

items.question: How is a prokaryotic cell different from a eukaryotic
items.answer:
Feature                   | Prokaryotic Cell           | Eukaryotic Cell
--------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------
Size                      | Small (1-10 micrometres)   | Large (5-100 micrometres)
Nuclear region            | Poorly defined; no nuclear | Well defined; nuclear
| membrane; called nucleoid  | membrane present
Chromosome number         | Single chromosome          | More than one chromosome
Membrane-bound organelles | Absent                     | Present (ER, Golgi,
|                            | mitochondria, etc.)
Examples                  | Bacteria                   | Plant cells, animal cells,
|                            | fungi

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which organelle is known as the "powerhouse of the cell"?
items.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP (energy currency) through cellular respiration and are called the powerhouse. Lysosomes are "suicide bags"; Golgi is the packaging centre; nucleus is the control centre.

items.question: Chloroplasts are important for:
items.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis in plant cells. Ribosomes do protein synthesis; mitochondria produce energy (ATP); nucleus controls cell division.

items.question: Lysosomes are called "suicide bags" because:

options.A: They produce energy for the cell
options.B: When they burst, their enzymes digest the cell itself

items.explanation: When lysosomes burst (in damaged cells), their powerful digestive enzymes are released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell itself, causing cell death.

items.question: Which of the following organelles is found only in plant cells?
items.explanation: Plastids (chloroplasts, leucoplasts, chromoplasts) are found only in plant cells. Mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, and ER are found in both plant and animal cells.

items.question: The central vacuole of a plant cell may occupy what percentage of the cell volume?
items.explanation: The central vacuole of mature plant cells may occupy 50-90% of the cell volume. It is filled with cell sap and provides turgidity to the cell.

items.question: Ribosomes are present on the surface of:
items.explanation: Ribosomes are attached to the surface of ROUGH ER (RER), giving it a rough appearance. RER is involved in protein synthesis. SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid synthesis.

items.question: Where do proteins and lipids for cell membrane construction come from?
items.explanation: The endoplasmic reticulum produces proteins (RER) and lipids (SER) that are used for membrane biogenesis - building and maintaining all cell membranes. This is one of the key functions of the ER.

items.question: Which organelle is involved in the formation of lysosomes?
items.explanation: The Golgi apparatus is involved in the formation of lysosomes. Lysosomal enzymes are made by RER, then processed and packaged by the Golgi apparatus into lysosomes.

items.question: Detoxification of drugs and poisons in liver cells is performed by:
items.explanation: Smooth ER (SER) plays a crucial role in detoxifying many poisons and drugs in the liver cells of vertebrates. This is one of the specialised functions of SER. Lysosomes digest waste materials, not chemical detoxification.

items.question: An organelle that has both its own DNA and ribosomes is:
items.explanation: Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes, making them capable of synthesising some of their own proteins. Plastids also have this property. Golgi, lysosomes, and ER do not have their own DNA.

items.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the difference between chromoplasts and leucoplasts?

options.A: Chromoplasts store starch; leucoplasts perform photosynthesis
options.B: Chromoplasts are coloured and include chloroplasts; leucoplasts are colourless
options.C: Chromoplasts are found in animal cells; leucoplasts are found in plant cells
options.D: Chromoplasts are in roots; leucoplasts are in leaves

items.explanation: Chromoplasts are coloured plastids; those with chlorophyll (green) are chloroplasts (for photosynthesis). Leucoplasts are white/colourless plastids whose primary function is storage (starch, oils, protein granules). Both are found only in plant cells.

items.question: If a cell's mitochondria are destroyed, which immediate consequence would occur?

options.B: Cell cannot produce ATP for energy-requiring activities

items.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP (energy currency). Without mitochondria, no ATP is produced, stopping all energy-requiring activities: active transport, muscle contraction, protein synthesis, etc. Photosynthesis needs chloroplasts; digestion of foreign particles needs lysosomes; protein transport needs ER/Golgi.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: New cells are formed in organisms in order to:
(i) Grow
(ii) Replace old, dead, and injured cells
(iii) Form gametes required for reproduction
The process by which new cells are made is called CELL DIVISION.
TWO MAIN TYPES of cell division:
(a) MITOSIS: process of cell division by which most cells divide for growth.
Each mother cell divides to form TWO identical daughter cells.
Daughter cells have the SAME NUMBER of chromosomes as the mother cell.
Helps in growth and repair of tissues in organisms.
(b) MEIOSIS: type of cell division in reproductive organs/tissues.
Produces FOUR new cells (instead of just two).
New cells only have HALF the number of chromosomes of the mother cell.
These reduced-chromosome cells (gametes) after fertilisation give rise to offspring.
Involves TWO CONSECUTIVE DIVISIONS.
